utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, I'm sorry you were all kept waiting but one of our members had a hospital appointment which took longer than anticipated however we are now ready. What we'll do is sit now until about quarter to 12.00, take a quarter of an hour break and then sit for the rest of the morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, would you please state your full name for the Trial Chamber and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Anto Puljic. I am from Kresevo in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was born in 1958.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can go relatively quickly through your personal information. In 1990, you became involved in the organising of a local branch of the main Croat political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Throughout 1991, we can say that you were an active member of the HDZ-BiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In my -- in 1990, it was still an illegal organisation and the municipal board of the HDZ was founded in Kresevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In April 1992, you moved from Kresevo to Busovaca where you spent about two months, and there you participated in the preparation of defence against the threat of the Bosnian Serb army attack or the JNA attack?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Their honours have had an opportunity to hear about it but maybe we can just restate it briefly. The Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina later were organised into Croat Defence Council in order to protect themselves?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: During the initial stages in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO was a hybrid organisation?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I could say that the HVO was a nucleus of both the military organisation and the civilian structure because the need of people in those areas were real. So one had to organise the education of health care and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In respect of that, in late spring and early summer 1992, you organised supplies of food and other things which were directed towards the defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After your short stay in Busovaca in June 1992, you returned to your home town Kresevo and resumed work in the company called TAO until the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In early January, 1993, president of the HVO executive, Dr. Jadranko Prlic appointed you to the position of the chief of defence administration in Travnik. You stayed in this position until the end of the war, that is until June of 1994.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I requested to step down, and I sent this request in to the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can come back to that later. But as a chief of defence administration in Travnik, you worked on the recruitment of new soldiers, mobilisation of people, acquisition of materials and equipment and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the scope of work of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. We can say a few words about the defence administration in Travnik. Could you state for the Trial Chamber very briefly what was the defence department in Travnik part of, and what were the subordinate bodies over which you had authority?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: The defence administration in Travnik operated as an administrative body of the defence department in the territory of Central Bosnia so it was a territorially administrative body of the defence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps we can clarify for the Trial Chamber, maybe just remind them. The defence department was one of the departments within the civilian segment of the HVO, some kind of a government headed by Mr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and this administration had jurisdiction over Central Bosnia. Under it were municipal offices through which it carried out its tasks as provided for by the decree on the armed forces. And let me clarify further, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This was something similar to the police administration within the department of the interior. It operated in a similar fashion except that we had our own tasks and the police department had their own scope of activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. We just said that above you was the defence department which was engaged in activities such as ministries usually do and you, yourself, you coordinated the activities of offices in various municipalities so you coordinated between the municipal offices and the defence department?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I reported to the head of the defence department and after it grew and developed into a full ministry, then I reported to the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: At the time when you were the head of the defence administration in Travnik, where was its -- where was the seat of the defence department?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: It was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And who was its head at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, the Travnik defence administration was superior to all the municipal offices including all offices in the Lasva Valley: Travnik, Novi Travnik, Busovaca and Vitez municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You were the head of this defence administration throughout the worst period, from January 1993 until the end of hostilities in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can ask the registry to please show the witness Z696 for the witness. I have a copy so maybe we can just lay it on the ELMO. It may be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, in the middle of 1993 the war escalated in Central Bosnia. Can you please first tell the Trial Chamber who attacked whom, and who attacked whom in Zenica, more specifically, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: The attack was carried out by the so-called Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the territory controlled by the HVO, and it attacked the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you at that time have any information about the events in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: That was the time when Vitez was on fire and Zenica also. We had very dramatic information arising from various sources about killings, woundings, setting homes on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: According to your information, how many Croats fled Zenica in April?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: The information that we received was that about 13.000 Croats were on the move, trying to cross into the territory controlled by the HVO, in two main directions. One was over Nako [phoen]. They were protected by the Jure Francetic Brigade Battalion. So people were protected as they were withdrawing and being evacuated to the areas where they felt more safe. And the other was via Vjetrenica to the area of Cajdras, where unfortunately elements of the Zenica Brigade were unable to effect a breakthrough. So we had an unprotected civilian population there in the area who remained surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Speaking of the events in Cajdras, you will see on the monitor a letter, a document which was tendered by the Prosecution, Z696. Do you recall this document? Who drafted this document, and to whom was it sent?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I recall the letter very well, and the events of that time are indelibly set in my memory. I wrote this as an appeal for assistance to the Zenica Croats. I had sent it to the commander of the British Battalion, I think it was Colonel Stewart; to Jean-Pierre Thebault, who was with the EC monitors; and to the representatives of the International Community. I wrote the letter because in these traumatic moments I thought it necessary, because we had no power or we had no forces to help the population, and we were unable to avert the catastrophe with which this population was threatened. I wrote it and I signed it, but I thought that it would be even more effective, and I added Mr. Dario Kordic's name to it and Mr. Ignac Kostroman's signature because I considered myself new in my position and not familiar enough to the people to whom I had appealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In this document your signature is in the left corner. Is that your signature over the name?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I can also see that I signed on behalf of Mr. Kostroman and Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: There is a word "za," which is Croat for "on behalf of."

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't ask their permission to use their names, but knowing them and knowing their moral principles and their attitudes, I thought that they would have done the same if they were in the same position. At that time I was in Vitez and I did not know whether they were -- they were also sending similar letters out of Busovaca or elsewhere. Our communications were cut off and the fighting was ongoing around Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you didn't ask for their permission, but rather you did it on your own initiative, for the reasons you just explained.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A technical question now. This letter was drafted in the English language, and you don't speak English. I assume that you had drafted it in Croatian and then you had it translated.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I used the services of a young woman who spoke English and who was available at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move on to paragraph 10, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The events in April and the attack of the ABiH against the HVO -- in fact, perhaps we could go a step back. When the BSA and JNA jointly attacked Croats and Muslims, how many refugees from those areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina occupied by the Serbs moved to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: According to our estimates, about 100.000 Muslims alone came from Western Bosnia, the so-called Bosnian Krajina, and the areas of Eastern Bosnia along the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Militarily speaking, which lines did these refugees cross in order to arrive in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: We were holding the line at Jajce and Travnik, and that is where the refugees from Western Bosnia came, so they had to cross the lines operated by the HVO. Those arriving from Eastern Bosnia, from the right flank, so to speak, and who were moving towards Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica, that part of the front was also manned by the HVO around the Lepenica Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, in that period you were an active member of the HDZ, and later on you were professionally involved as the head of the defence administration in Travnik. And throughout this period, from 1991 to 1993, have you ever heard that within these provisional institutions that there was any official or unofficial policy of persecution of Muslims in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and later Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, in other words, in the territories under the military control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: There was no official policy, or unofficial policy, for that matter. These areas were inhabited by local Muslims too. And the Muslim refugees who arrived from Western and Eastern Bosnia, the demographic structure was upset. An imbalance was created, and pressure. It was an enormous pressure on the resources that we had. They were pushed to the limit. Several families were staying in a single home. In such difficult circumstances, we had problems with basic supplies. But there was no official or unofficial policy, and even if I had known of such, I would not have participated in it. It would have been insane to engage in ethnic cleansing of those proportions, given the population -- the size of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the population that was there. We are a small community, and it would even be illogical for us to have pursued such measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, you said that you felt enormous pressure on the resources that you had. The influx of various groups, which could not be fully controlled, did all that cause an increase in the crime rate, and did it increase the lawlessness in the territories?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The situation changed significantly. People who had some criminal tendencies and had criminal records also came with the refugees. Of course, the local police force was facing enormous problems, and the civilian HVO structures and the police tried to maintain law and order in this chaotic situation. There were many incidents: murders and robberies. The security situation deteriorated by this mass influx of people, and these people were not properly documented and our police was unable to track them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You said that the framework of social structure had just fallen apart?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that central government in Sarajevo was cut off, and all the institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina ground to a halt so we tried to raise it from the ashes, so to speak, with the resources of personnel that we had available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Talking about the crime, the looting and evictions and other crime, was it one-sided or was it spread in all communities?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: It was spread in all communities. It was difficult to say who was the more of a victim, whether the Croat or the Muslim population. It depended on where one was. Some criminal groups were operating not along the ethnic lines, but they were interethnic. And later, the later investigations revealed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is interesting that members of different ethnic groups would make part of the same criminal group.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps the -- just one more question on that topic. This criminal elements, the violence and acts of provocations, were all these part of an orchestrated policy which was imposed by the leadership or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No, these criminal groups which were active in some areas such as Sarajevo, Zenica, Banja Luka, only transferred to this other territory, the free territory and continued with the same type of activities which they had been engaged previously. This was not done by -- this was not coordinated by any leadership either at the local or regional levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We can move on to paragraph 12, Your Honours. Mr. Puljic, you have already answered to a degree that the authorities had all ground to a halt in view of the situation and all the operations, but tell us what happened to the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a party. Did it remain operational throughout 1992-1993 or was there an interruption in its activities?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: When the aggression broke out against Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, the HDZ froze its work, and I believe it was frozen throughout 1993, that is, as of the latter half of 1992 and in -- throughout 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You were the head of the defence administration, in other words you were a civilian you were not a military, but in view of your job, you also knew the personnel, I do not mean personnel as personnel, but persons who were performing different military duties. Tell us, please, did you ever hear that in the HVO, there was so-called polit commissars from the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, how shall I call it, deputies responsible for political work that would correspond with what existed in the former Soviet system as it is claimed in this case?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No, I am not aware -- well, in every brigade, that is, when the brigades were formed, in every brigade, there were departments, the IPD, departments for information and propaganda. But those were never influential people, people with weight, but rather men who, in the eyes of the brigade commands, could perform such duties. I knew a large number of those people because after all, the mobilisation was taking place through our offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, IPD services exist in other armies too, but would you say then that this propounded in this case, is it tenable, that these polit commissars existed in that they were people who had some commanding role?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. The commanding role in the brigade was played only by brigade commanders or commanders of units. I wouldn't be aware of anything like that in what you mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: As the head of the defence administration in Travnik, you covered the territory of Central Bosnia, and that is also the territory covered, roughly speaking, but the Central Bosnia Operative Zone headed by Commander Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Quite so. Our areas of responsibility largely overlapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And to round off this subject about so-called polit commissars, did you ever hear that any HDZ representative at any level ever issued any orders or commanded any unit in the area in which you were active?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: In the area in which I worked, the commanding duties rested with the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, that is, commander -- brigade commanders and other units subordinated to him. And never -- and some political individuals never had any opportunity of issuing orders because there was a very clear-cut system, a very clear chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So I suppose you never heard of any such case?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Puljic, a couple of questions about Mr. Kordic. You met him, I suppose, at that time when you began to prepare for the defence against the army of Bosnian Serbs, rather, the JNA at the time, so that was the period between 1990 onward?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, early 1990, I should say, or sometimes we would meet at meetings or at HDZ meetings. But then in 1991, as the situation, the security of political situation began to deteriorate in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we then began to meet more often because we thought that the gravity of the time required certain solutions, necessitated solutions, and that is why we had to meet more often. And then during the war, during the aggression, we met at meetings quite often so I can say that I know Mr. Kordic quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna was founded Mr. Kordic also discharged certain duties. Do you know what those duties in Herceg-Bosna were?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: When the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna was founded, Mr. Kordic was elected one of two vice-presidents. The president was Mr. Mate Boban, and vice-presidents, Mr. Dario Kordic and Mr. Bozo Rajic. I am aware of his role and his activities in the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Where was the -- where were the headquarters of your office or rather the Travnik defence administration in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: In 1993, for security reasons, our seat was in Vitez. Basically we were supposed to be in Travnik but because of the vicinity of the front and the daily shelling of Travnik by the Bosnian Serb army from Vlasic and Kumar, so that we decided that it would be better to move out and to all intents and purposes, we worked from Vitez, that is, we had this detached headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Naumovski, I'd like to ask the following of the witness, could he help us understand the situation better? He stated that there were the military commanders and that they have nothing to do with the politicians. Could you tell us what Mr. Mate Boban's role was? You've just mentioned him. He was the president of the Herceg-Bosna community. What was his role at the military level in relation to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mate Boban was the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and when the Croat Defence Council was founded, he became its supreme commander. He was the supreme commander. Only he could issue orders to the commander or rather to the main staff. And then the main staff issued orders to units in Operative Zones, and one of those zones was Central Bosnia. I believe there were three Operative Zones, but I'm not sure whether there were three or four. One was in Tomislavgrad, one was in Mostar, I mean the seats, and I believe there was one in Posavina. I'm not sure about that one. I'm not sure about the status. It could have been -- because that did not fall within my field of jurisdiction and I was not really interested in finding that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this being so, could we say that as far as Mr. Mate Boban was concerned, there was some confusion that he had at the same time a political and a military power?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Well, he was the head of the Croat Defence Council until at some point, the civilian wing, the civilian arm separated and then Mr. Jadranko Prlic became the prime minister, and he remained the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and the supreme commander of the armed forces. I do not know, Your Honour, if I managed to explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question was as follows: I wanted to know whether it could be said about Mr. Mate Boban that he had, at some point in time, a political and a military authority or power.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case what was the vice-president role, namely the role of Mr. Kordic as such?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic played a political role only, that is, the commander over the Croat Defence Council rested with the president. That is what the documents of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna say after the aggression began against Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Kordic did not have the authority over the armed forces of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, aren't you aware that military power or authority may have been delegated by Mr. Boban to Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Such an authority was never transmitted, I mean, to command units, nor did I have an opportunity to do so, nor do I know that Mr. Kordic ever issued an order, nor would any commander ever comply with such an order. Because only the commander of the Operative Zone could issue such orders, that is, the person who at that particular moment held that office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, perhaps we could mention another detail to clarify for His Honour. Under the decree on the armed forces, the supreme commander of the armed forces is the president as you have just told us.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And that degree does not mention deputies of the supreme commander. Such office does not exist.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I mean, in the decree on the armed forces, there's not a single mention of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers reminds me it was D172/1 [as interpreted], tabs 7 and 20, Defence Exhibit. 182/1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, I was about to ask you -- that is, you told us that the headquarters of your administration had been relocated to Vitez. Which building did you move into?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: We were in the Vitez Hotel. We were there. A suite was placed at our disposal. And for the duration of the war we were given yet another small room, and that is where we organised the minimal work to enable us to function, so that we could release as many people for the armed forces, or rather for the command of individual brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: As you went to work, day in and day out, you must have also seen people who came to the seat of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. So tell us: Did Mr. Kordic come to the Operative Zone often or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Kordic in the hotel from time to time, or rather seldom. He would come to meetings of a broad nature to discuss perhaps the security situation or political situation. At a particular point in time, because the crisis in that area lasted from 1992 through 1993 and even 1994, and that was the period of time when I used to meet him from time to time, when meetings would be convened, because there was a hall -- there was a conference hall in the hotel. There were facilities there which would enable a number of people to attend, I mean people who came from the political, that is, from the executive branch, and I would attend them as the head of the administration, of the police administration, and so on and so forth. That would be -- those were the occasions when I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So if I can conclude from what you say, those were some special occasions, that is, some joint meetings convened in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. A while ago you answered Judge Bennouna that Mr. Kordic did not make part of the chain of command and that he could not issue any orders. But tell us: In those early days of organisation, Mr. Kordic -- did Mr. Kordic play a certain role, say, in 1992, while there was still fierce fighting going on around Jajce, and so on and so forth? Do you remember any of his activities at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic's role, by and large, he was a local, a regional politician, and he regularly made himself heard as the voice of the people, and he followed the activities and operations in Central Bosnia, and he would then become committed as a politician. And when we worked clandestinely, he also tried to help and organise, as I did. But as for the issue of any orders, no, he did not do any, because at that time there were municipal staffs, so the chain of command went through municipal staffs. I'm referring to the time before brigades were formed, so that he did not have any command role at that time either. What is, for instance, very typical of the Jajce front, because the HVO members in Jajce were investing tremendous effort and tried to reorganise the unit by bringing in units from other municipalities. And since in the early days the results were very meager, because in 1992 everything was based on the principle of voluntarily -- everything was based on volunteers, and people were not really applying to join. So that Mr. Kordic joined in, called meetings, called upon the activists and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. municipal staffs and their associates, held press conferences. And in different papers, municipal organs that we were starting at the time, he wrote for them, so that of course people began to respond. More people responded to our calls for volunteers, and that was how we could help those who were fighting the defence in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So he encouraged people to volunteer; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is precisely it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And in his political work, including what you just told us about, did you ever hear Mr. Kordic voice any extremist or offensive, insulting view about some other ethnic group or people, and I mean Muslims too?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I never heard him, nor do I think that Mr. Kordic ever said anything like that, because we met at a time when we were losing sometimes as many as 100 men a day in those conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But even in those difficult times, that is, when we were on the defensive, he never voiced any such view, either in conversations or in his public addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Puljic: In those early days initially, when Mr. Kordic and you were involved in this initial organisation of the HVO, you also did it as volunteers. And when each of you was responsible for his particular aspect of work, did you or Mr. Kordic have any military experience regarding the defence or anything?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Kordic did not have any kind of expertise except regular service with the former JNA, and the same applies to me too: no military expertise, so that I could not really become involved in that segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. But in those early days, you and Mr. Kordic were involved in military matters exclusively, or were you involved in that other segment which had to do with the initial organisation of the defence, that is, logistics, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Our field of -- our jurisdiction had to do only with the logistics, that is, Mr. Kordic, in the segment of encouraging people to join in, those who were -- who had expertise and knowledge and, shall I say, courage to join in. That was in the logistics, absolutely, because I personally -- a large part of activities in the segment for which I was responsible would not have been able to carry out without support and commitment to Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Puljic, the last topic, which is paragraph 16, is the last subject that I wanted to ask you something about. As the chief of the defence administration and defence offices subordinated to you, you were involved in mobilisation; and you worked, as we have just said, within the defence department of the HVO, with the seat in Mostar for a while?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Subsequently, because of the combat operations in Mostar, it was relocated to Citluk and Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. You know that some soldiers born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there were some Croats among them, but Muslims as well, served with the Croatian army in the beginning, during the aggression of the JNA against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am aware of that. And I even knew quite a number of those individuals, because there were among them neighbours of mine, so I knew quite a number of those members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Is it true that some of those people who volunteered to defend the Republic of Croatia against the aggression, that is, that some of those men returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina when the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: My assessments say that over 85 per cent of those men returned and joined the units of the Croat Defence Council to help, because they were already lads with war experience, so that their help was precious. Their status, what was their status in the Croatian army, we were not aware of that. But with us there were members of the Croat Defence Council. They reported individually. They did not come as a combat group, what we call -- that is, groups of three; they reported individually. Whenever they could, sometimes they were given leave or some -- at times simply left their HV units and came.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you admitted those men in your ranks because, after all, they were on your records, since their birthplaces were in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You do not know what their status was in the Republic of Croatia and you never went into it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No, we did not go into it, because that was not within our jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us: Throughout this time, throughout 1993 until the spring of 1994, while you were the chief of the defence administration in Travnik, in the territory in which you were active were there any Croatian army units, or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: There were no units. I have just said so. When those military conscripts were coming back from Croatian units, they do not come to us as organised or as combat groups; they came as individuals to us. So that there were no units, not even of a combat group, which is usually three- to five-men strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Puljic. Your Honours, I have no further questions in my examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puljic.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I shall now ask you some questions on behalf of Mr. Mario Cerkez, whom I represent in this case. We have just heard from you that in early 1993 you became the chief of the Travnik Defence Administration, with headquarters in Vitez, in the Vitez Hotel, which also housed the headquarters of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Puljic, look at a graph and comment on the graph that I will show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the graph which was used in the Blaskic case, and it will help us to illustrate the subject that I should like to address. [In English] And one can be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This Defence Exhibit shall be marked D69/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, here on this chart we see in the upper corner the mark of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. And to translate it into a more understandable language for all of us, that means practically the government of the HZ HB. The government has several departments, that is, ministries, and one of them is the department, that is, the Ministry of Defence, and you were one of the civil servants in that department; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So tell us: Which were the subdepartments of the defence department? What was its structure, its layout?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I wasn't quite aware of the organisational layout of it. I was familiar with the civilian wing. But I don't quite understand this chart. I do not think that this chart is complete, and it can show only the chain of command. But otherwise, yes; yes, that is how one could take this chart, as kind of a teaching aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But within this Department of Defence, there was the civilian segment, and you were part of this. So what did it do?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: It did work having to do with recruitment, military records, mobilisation, because mobilisation for certain things could be done by this subdepartment. For instance, in case it came to some large complexes or factories, and things -- and some major resources. I'm mentioning it as an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, when you say "mobilisation," you mean that some facilities which are civilian are placed under the management of military units in case of a war or threat of war?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The role of this subdepartment for civilian issues is mobilisation, that is, people mobilisation, and sending of -- posting of people to units and assignment of facilities to units. That is what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I'm going to interrupt. Can you tell us, please, about this chart which you've produced? Where does it come from, please, so that we can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This chart was used in the Blaskic case, and its function in my questioning is really as an aid, just to facilitate our understanding of what the witness is talking about. It does not pretend to be an exact chart, but it can still be elucidated through evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And who produced it in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So far as I know, it was the Defence for Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And can you help us as to the witness who produced it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honours, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt it can be further elucidated. As far as this witness is concerned, he cannot help with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Your Honours, and I do not expect the witness to confirm the accuracy of this chart, but I rather wanted to use it as a guide. And if I may, I only had two more questions related to this chart. With your permission, I would still like to ask them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, only two additional questions in respect of this. If you look at the left and right from the middle box which is called the main headquarters or main staff, we see the SIS and the military police. They are directly linked to the defence department, does that correspond to what you knew?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: When you asked me the first question, I am not entirely sure and I am not entirely familiar with this functioning and at what stage it functioned in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, then, Mr. Puljic, we will not pursue this any further. We're moving on to the next topic. You told us that the defence departments which were in municipalities also were for recruitment and filling in the complements of units. You may be aware that Mr. Mario Cerkez -- and the Trial Chamber knows -- is aware of this -- was appointed the commander of Vitez Brigade by an order of General Blaskic sometime in March of 1993. Do you know this and do you know that immediately before this appointment, the Vitez Brigade was established?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I had to know these things because the Operative Zone commands asked of us to provide personnel for the newly-established brigade, and I needed to know by virtue of my job what -- so that I could issue specific orders to my associates and to my subordinates in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. And we're talking about end of March 1993. You had an insight into the Vitez Brigade and its manpower.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: The Vitez Brigade had the strength of one battalion, I think about 600 men, because it was to be like a field brigade whose full strength would have been 2.000 men. But given the population and the situation, we could not expect that, but 500 to 600 men is what we had. That would have been the commanding staff, communications and all the structure that was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Given the numbers, such a brigade, theoretically speaking, would have had to number some 2.000 men as its full complement and it was only filled to the size of 500, 600 men which meant about 25 to 30 per cent of its full theoretical complement?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, mathematically speaking, I think your estimate is about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your experience in peace time circumstances, how much time would be needed to fill such a unit and bring it to its full level?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I think that the activities involving that would have taken about three to four months. If you started out with the establishment logs and went all the way, it would take about that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. In your evidence, you said that starting in 1992 and on, the HVO held the positions facing Bosnian Serbs and other forces who attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that the assistance for this defence was coming from all municipalities who were affected. Are you aware that assistance was also coming from the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: The two months that I spent in Busovaca in 1992 is what I can speak to. And then in 1993, while I was in my duty, I know that the Vitez units were also involved in those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that in one shift, about 70 to 100 men were sent from Vitez to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I did not know about the formation and the size of manpower, and it was not my role to know how many members of each specific unit were being sent to the front lines. Some of it we could gauge from the logistics that were required.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But in your estimate, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I really cannot be very accurate there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, then, Mr. Puljic. But do you know that on the very day of 16 April when there was combustion in Vitez and surroundings that one of such units was left stranded in the area of Turbe?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I know that because we did not know the fate of that unit. I think it could have been the size of a platoon if my recollection is correct on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, when you came in the position which you then carried out for a while and that was in the forward post in Vitez, I assume that you also cooperated closely with Marijan Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Marijan Skopljak was my point person in Vitez. He was the head of the Vitez office and of course I had to deal with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So he was the person who worked on these activities for the military needs such as recruitment mobilisation and so on?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Marijan Skopljak, in October of 1993, was removed from his duties; is that correct? Blanked page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1993 from the establishment of the office, he showed certain weaknesses in the organisational work and even stepped outside of the scope of his work. We were not happy with his performance, we asked the minister to replace him and he was then replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened after his dismissal, who was put in his position?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Given the weaknesses at that time, Mr. Stipo Zigonjic, who was also part of that structure was not promoted. We had a problem. We discussed what we should do. I talked to General Blaskic and we asked that the Vitez Brigade take over part of that job. We wanted them to do that in the interim period, but it dragged on for two months and only in December was the new head appointed. And since the Vitez Brigade, through the cooperation with -- which we had with them showed that it had a very good personnel and we were -- we asked them to take over that system of carrying out these duties. And General Blaskic gave an order to Mr. Cerkez and I also, as a head of the district of the defence administration, gave my own order to the office to have them carry out those jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In other words, did the situation force you to mingle the military and the civilian aspects of the -- that work?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This may be perhaps a good moment to break for the morning break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How much longer do you anticipate being, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now until five to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Puljic, before the adjournment, we were talking about the situation that you described, the dismissal of Marijan Skopljak and that is what resulted in the overlapping of military and civilian structures. I should like to ask you to look at a document which concerns Mr. Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nodded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And I should like to ask you to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be numbered Defence exhibit D70/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, you see that document. It says Department of Defence, then it says defence administration Vitez. It is a decision authorising Mr. Pero Skopljak to perform, be in charge of the duties relative to -- I don't know -- and so on and so forth, and negotiations with the international organisations. The document was issued by Anto Valenta who was a civil servant and co-signed by Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, the commander of the Operative Zone. Is that one of the examples of what we just talked about?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: All I can say is this: Mr. Blaskic had to give his consent so that Mr. Skopljak could be taken into account because then many civilians, that is, many men who were for exchange, whether there were any unit members, I'm not sure and I cannot comment about that, but I know about civilians had to go into areas where they were accommodated, sheltered from combat activities. Because you see at that date, at that time, Vitez is up in flames, and slowly, a front line is being established. And now one has to see what can one do with civilians who, because of combat operations, had to seek shelter. I believe it was the cinema in the Croat centre in Vitez and several places where the conditions were satisfactory. So Mr. Skopljak needed to have the consent of Mr. Blaskic so the certain commanders could then comply with this. This paper originated, if I may add, it just happened to be written on the letterhead of the defence department because Mr. Skopljak's office was not yet being established because things did not function at the time just to explain that there was no overlapping of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. But Mr. Pero Skopljak was a civilian, and that is unquestionable.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And he was appointed to coordinate various public activities and he also took care of the prisoners of war at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A while ago, Mr. Puljic, you mentioned that this document originated at a time when Vitez was up in flames, as you put it. We know that the attack on Vitez happened on the 16th of April, 1993. You have told us that from -- you told us whether the units were all in full strength, and we realise that they were far from it. So the situation required -- made additional mobilisation necessary. Could you tell us if the commander of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia, Colonel Blaskic, on the 16th of April, in the afternoon hours, ordered and requested supplementary mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I already told you that we had the determined the dynamics of activities, of how the brigade should be replenished, and this decree also made the time schedule. But since there was this attack on Vitez, since war happened, then of course we had to cut down the intervals in which mobilisation would be conducted so as to somehow respond to this threat posed to the area of responsibility of the Vitez Brigade. I can confirm it. I mean, he really was in a situation where he had to request supplementary mobilisation; that is that those activities which had been agreed upon earlier should be cut short and finished as quickly as possible; if possible, within one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. But we're referring to the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, in your department, or rather in your office, there was also the so-called wartime production. That was one of the segments?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But a correction. I have to make a correction. I was the head of the Defence Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, my mistake. Will you please explain to us in a couple of sentences: What does the term "wartime production" mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: After the stock was taken of the situation in the end of June, or rather in early May, the political and security situation that was under consideration at that time brought to light the fact that not all resources were used for the -- to meet the needs of the defence war: Industrial capacities in Travnik, free part of Novi Travnik and Busovaca. And the situation required from us to put it all under one umbrella, under one system, so as not to disperse the energy. And at one of the meetings I was ordered -- that is, I was issued instructions -- I was instructed to conceive the system of administration; and I did that and I made a proposal, and that was submitted to Mr. Stojic and he approved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. So this wartime production was organised within the Defence Department. No. Defence Administration, sorry. Defence Administration. And it was yet another civilian segment?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely, a civilian segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Even though, at the end of the story, it was to serve armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: True, yes, but this involved also things that were made, manufactured for hospitals, for health centres, for the population, and everything. But what we needed to do was to focus the energy, because there was a crisis within the area, and we had to do it and use the available resources more rationally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then you appointed your assistant to supervise this?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was Mr. Marko Lujic, called Markesa, who was responsible for the civilian production.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And to sum it up, then, so he was your assistant for wartime production, that is, a civilian who did that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, you, by definition, spent the worst moments of it all in Vitez. You communicated with many people, and I also suppose that you communicated with Mr. Cerkez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and repeatedly so, because one of the matters of work I adopted was to talk directly to commanders of individual units who were within the field of competence of the Defence Department; that is, to provide the logistics, to receive the information, of course, from heads of those offices, but also to have the feedback information from those units, so that Mr. Cerkez and I and his associates met quite often to discuss the replenishments and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. In your contacts with Mr. Cerkez, did you ever hear him advocate, promote discrimination of other ethnic groups or speak about other ethnic groups, and I mean Muslims in particular, to belittle them, to insult them, and things like that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard anything like it, nor is that how I understood his mental frame. I do not think he would have ever been able to. You understand. And I also know, among other things, that he had to take care about the safety of a Muslim woman who I believe was a midwife in Vitez. This is just an example, and there is a number of such examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Puljic. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, I've got a number of questions to ask you. Let's just start off with some general things, please. Your tasks were entirely civilian, is that correct; there was nothing military about what you did?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you answered to whom?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I answered to the chief of the Department of Defence, and later the minister of the Ministry of Defence, once the government of the Herceg Republic -- of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So -- right. The next thing is: The HVO Main Staff -- and I'm simply looking at a document that was shown to you, although you didn't seem to know much about it. But the HVO Main Staff is a military body and is also a part of the Department of Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No. It is not part of the Defence Department. It could be done vertically through the Defence Department. But in terms of its functions, it accounted to -- it was answerable to the president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But certainly the HVO Main Staff, as this diagram, 69/2, if it remains an exhibit, shows, the HV --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The HVO Main Staff was the body that commanders of Operative Zones 1 and 2 answered to?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So there's no doubt about HVO Main Staff being a military body?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council was definitely a military body, and it looked after individual units within the field of its competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand how your work, which was plainly closely related to military matters, would be integrated with the military matters themselves. From what you've told us, and correct me if I've got it wrong, you've got to go right the way up to the level of Department of Defence before you can find someone who has responsibility for both your civilian side and the Main Staff military side. Is that really correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm afraid that I wasn't understood very well. The Main Staff was responsible only for subordinated units, that is, military formations of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you, as --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: And if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Will you please allow me to finish. And the ministry, that is, the Defence Department, had several segments, including a civilian segment, and I -- and that was the segment that I worked in. And it was responsible for the mobilisation, military records, recruitment, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think I did misunderstand you. If we think of the thing conceptually, it's only at the level of the Ministry of Defence -- or the Department of Defence, whatever it is -- that you have someone to whom both your non-military side and the military side are both answerable. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I was -- in my segment of work, I accounted [as interpreted] the minister, or rather -- that is, head of the Defence Department, subsequently the minister, and to me were accountable the subordinate groups, that is, heads of defence departments -- defence offices. They could not communicate with the minister directly --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: -- without my authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because you tell us there's this complete separation between civil and military departments, it presumably wouldn't be correct for your department to be communicating directly with the military departments locally, would it? You wouldn't be able to do that without the approval of the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: The decree regulating the competence of the Defence Department and the rules of work and competence of all segments of the Defence Department are clearly defined, so that we -- with regard to units, that is, brigades in the area of responsibility of this administration, there was no chain of command, so to speak; the cooperation was horizontal. That is, we were to send them men, resources, vehicles, facilities, so on and so forth, which they requested from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that at the local level, your civilian wing and the military wing were in fact entirely integrated; you dealt with them directly.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Hierarchically, not down the chain of command. But our role was to turn over men and materiel to the units, and that would be the end of our activities. And as for the troops and resources who had been turned over to the units, then those units became responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. One other very general point at this stage. We know that the Main Staff was a military organisation. What's a forward command post? Can you just enlighten us, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: The command post is a military term, so the terminology -- for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. purpose of some combat operations, the chief of the Main Staff is relocated, or the commander of the Operative Zone, or commander -- that is, from their regular seat, when -- because of the vicinity of the front line, and he then moves closer to his area of responsibility, from which he runs individual operations, whether it be combats or something else. And we also used this term even though -- not in our official correspondence, but even the administration was -- had also been relocated; that is, our seat was in Travnik, but we worked and lived in Vitez all the time because of the situation on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the very beginning of matters you've told us about, namely, the setting up of the Community of Herceg-Bosna -- first of all, setting up of the political party, HDZ, you were actually quite a central player there, weren't you? You were a main board member; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I was not a member. I was in a municipal organisation in Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Kresevo, incidentally, is that where Kostroman comes from?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kostroman comes from Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you a friend of his?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: We knew each other. We worked together in the same company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right, that's fine, thank you. I'm not going to take the witness to them but --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I finish? May I finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless it's relevant, Mr. Puljic. As you will understand, we are very short of time. Now, if you want to say something that is relevant about Mr. Kostroman, you can, but could you keep your answers, on the whole, as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to take the witness to it. But it's right, isn't it, that you were present in those early meetings in July of 1991 in Busovaca and Vitez where the party was set up?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: What period of time do you have in mind? I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: July 1991 and then again in January of 1992 you were present at the meetings.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: The HDZ was founded in 1990. And Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna is a territorial organisation, it is not a political organisation. So it is a segment. It covered an area of interest and its purpose was to resolve certain matters that had arisen at that time. I was a member of the municipal board of Kresevo so I was at the meeting as a representative of Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Let's just turn, briefly, to Mr. Kordic since he was also at those meetings. You tell us that he wasn't doing anything military, but what actually was he doing?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic and other people who attended those meetings in view of the crisis which was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the political and every other crisis, we had to discuss and think as serious and responsible men what were we to do under the circumstances so those were political meetings --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question probably wasn't helpful. It's my fault not yours. Right from the beginning, and right until 1994, I want to have a thumbnail sketch of what Mr. Kordic was doing, and let me just narrow the question for you in this way: Once you had your job, you had a specific function to do. You had lots of letters to write and orders to make, and whatever else and so on. People who have a ministry to run, they have a portfolio of functions to perform and so on. We can see what they had to do. Now, what, please, did Mr. Kordic do between 1992, say, and 1994? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was our regional leader, political leader. He grew up from the people as the voice of the people. He followed all the developments in Central Bosnia in particular, but also in Bosnia-Herzegovina and even on a broader area, and communicated. And as the voice of the people, he endeavored to marshal the energy and to work politically because those were very difficult times. He was trying to calm down the situation and also. So this was his field of competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was effectively, the region's political leader; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Quite so. He was well -- how shall we put it -- perhaps the popular tribune. The people's tribune whom people trusted and who articulated very well the needs of the people at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you remember His Honour Judge Bennouna asked you a question about Mr. Boban and so on. Forget the formalities of the documents that may have come into existence. Is the reality of the history, and we can deal with this quite shortly, that Mr. Kordic was either Mr. Boban's practical deputy in your region or, alternatively, he was, as it were, Mr. Boban, himself, in your region. What do you say to those two possibilities?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't think I really got what you meant. Could you please repeat the question? It's very broad and I didn't really get it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he -- first of all, was he the practical, the real deputy of Boban in your region?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic, after his admission to the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, he was one of its vice-presidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know, and I've asked you, please, to forget about all the bits of paper and the rules and the regulations and to tell us in real terms what he was. Was he, for all practical purposes, Boban's deputy in your region?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: He could not be Boban's deputy. He was the vice-president and the first, the leading political individual there. He could only act in the field of politics, and that is the field that he acted within.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Nice. I'd like to ask this of the witness following the question and the answer. Now, what does it entail, in your view, to be a vice-president? What does it entail to be a vice-president regarding Mr. Kordic? What does that mean being a vice-president? Does it have a substance?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the substance of Mr. Kordic's work is of political nature, that is, no activity neither through the executive power structure nor through the military segment. Mr. Kordic had no competencies nor did Mr. Bozo Rajic. I am not referring to the rules, I am talking about real life. That is how it was in real life. That is my experience, and that is what I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first answer, of course, was to take us back to the rules and regulations but it's right, isn't it, that the role of, I think you described him as "tribune" is in no way allowed for in the rules of Herceg-Bosna or the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, is it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. Can you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you describe Mr. Kordic's role in translation the word "tribune" was used, and I'm suggesting to you that that role that you articulated for us is, itself, in no way identified or established in the rules.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: You said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying that Mr. Kordic's role in various things he did is actually fully identified in the rules and regulations of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: He was vice-president and he was only active in political affairs as a leader, as a political leader. He was active as such in that area. I hope that now I clarified sufficiently the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I still don't actually have a picture of what it was he was doing. I'll come back to that in a minute, but just confirm for us, please, he was a man young enough to be in the forces himself. He was of military age; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Once the war in full started, what -- can we have a picture, what was he doing all day long? He wasn't sending letters. He wasn't receiving letters very much. What was he doing all day long?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Listen, Mr. Kordic, as a politician was receiving delegations, I assume. At least on the occasions when I was there, delegations from municipalities of Central Bosnia, people talked to him, and we all analysed situations, the security. He tried to be politically active in calming down the situation in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But presumably if anybody came to him with a military problem, he'd have to say, "Not me, go somewhere else." Is that right? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if anybody came to him with any military problems. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But he wouldn't have any power to deal with them in any event, would he?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know why he was surrounded by armed military men? Do you know why that happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I explained the security situation, I previously talked about that. With the influx of about -- over 100.000 refugees, and with them came people who were potential criminals, there were murderers. The situation in the area had worsened significantly and he -- as a political leader, I think that it's normal anywhere in the world that politicians have security details, let alone in the critical times such as the one when Mr. Kordic was active.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to deal with documents chronologically, but in light of one of your answers, to His Honour Judge Bennouna, I'm going to take one document out of sequence. It's still your position, is it, that he never operated in any way as Boban's deputy, anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: He could have only been involved in things as a political figure. Blanked page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And as specific tasks are concerned, if Mr. Boban talked to Mr. Kordic, I don't know about that. I was not in a position to have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we look, please, at Exhibit 1208, the original coming your way. You see now this is a document dated the 20th of September 1993. If we look at the original just to check it, it's got your name and it's got your signature. If we come back to the body of the document if you'd be good enough to follow it in the original while we just summarise it in reading it in English. It's a document that's an order about conscripts conforming compulsory work at a factory. Conscripts securing the plant, about the premises and plants of that factory to be sealed in the presence of the factory's security commander. That order to enter into force and the commander of the Viteska Brigade, the head of the Novi Travnik defence office to be responsible for its execution. Now what are you going to say, this is a civilian matter or a military matter or both?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I have to be more comprehensive in answering this question, with the Chamber's permission. We had established a department for military production and we had started it. We looked in the personnel, and looked at the situation, the terrain, the security situation, and it was determined that we had to engage in these activities which are purely civilian. The defence office's work was, at that time, already discharged by the Vitez Brigade, and we sent this as information and an order. It was sent to the defence offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I know this document very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is what is on the signature page? You told us what a forward command post is so we know. Kordic is signing now as the head of the forward command post of the office of the president of the republic. What is that, if it isn't the de facto deputy to the president, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I use this from the media. It was never done officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: In the official correspondence. This would never appear with this heading, but at that time, the forward post of the office of the president was used. It doesn't mean that it was correctly used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said something about --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: And the reason, if I can just add, the reason why I named these individuals was to reinforce the implementation of this order because I was not sure that without them, I would be able to enforce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said something about using this from the media and I wanted you to clarify that so that we can understand what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: You see there were press conferences where Mr. Kordic spoke, and that was covered in the local media because we had a media blockade at the time so each municipality had their own media outlets. And so I may have picked it up somewhere in passing. After all, this is -- this doesn't have any stamp of his or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It seems to have been signed by him, Mr. Puljic.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did sign it. I asked for his signature so that I would get -- so that this order would have a greater authority and see this is going to the civilian sector. This is the SPS plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that I can understand what you're saying and so that I've got it clear, you are saying you put down a title that you knew to be false and Mr. Kordic signed it when it was manifestly false, or did you put down a title that was manifestly true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I think that when Mr. Kordic was signing this, I'm not sure that he had that title. But he didn't pay, in fact -- yes, I think that you used a good word there. Because he was, without a doubt, a political leader and nobody would have paid any attention, nor was it significant to anyone what his position was as quoted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you about to say that he didn't pay any attention to what he signed and then changed your mind about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I did not change my mind. His name was what was important, and the authority that it carried at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's look at Exhibit 1209 just very quickly. The same day, this order deals with activities specified in Article 14 on the armed forces about things that had been entrusted to the Vitez Brigade. It deals with employees of the Vitez defence office reporting immediately to the commander of the Vitez Brigade for deployment. It says that the chief of the office shall turn over the affairs and documentation to the commander of the Vitez Brigade. It then says that the Vitez Brigade shall discharge the affairs of the defence office. So shall we say this is, at the very least, mixed military and civilian topics?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This is a conclusion that you drew. That is not what I said, but when asked by Counsel Naumovski, sorry, Counsel Mikulicic, I pointed out the circumstances under which we produced such a document in assessing the overall situation and the weaknesses of the Vitez office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
