utterances.text: But the point again and very quickly and I'm going to move on now, Kordic, by the way, he's signing as a colonel on both occasions, he's signs as the forward command post for the president because he was a military man, and in the same way that Boban was commander in chief of the forces, he was reflecting his authority as a person with command over the forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No, you drew an absolutely wrong conclusion. Mr. Kordic was a politician, a political figure, and he never could issue an order to a unit. Even here, he did not issue an order. It was my order as the head of the defence administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us, Mr. Puljic, what was the forward command post of the office of the president of the Republic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I cannot explain that. When I mentioned the forward command post, I was referring to the forward command posts of the Main Staff, the district headquarters, or local headquarters, operative zones, but I cannot tell you about this one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What had you intended to mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: My intention was for Mr. Kordic, given the circumstances under which this order was sent to the defence offices. Because there was also an order of the Operative Zone command, Tihomir Blaskic. In coordination with me, he issued an order to the Vitez Brigade commander to take over those duties, because the life couldn't stop; we needed to have the flow of personnel and materiel. So we had to move these activities to the Vitez Brigade until we appointed a new head of the defence office, and our assessment was that we were not going to be able to do that very fast. And we needed personnel and we needed materiel, equipment, every day, on a daily basis. Given the overall political situation in Vitez municipality at the time, the political insecurity situation, we thought that he could be -- that he could agree. So I asked Mr. Valenta Kostroman and Kordic to also lend their support, because I thought that it would be reinforced. But I was the one who issued it. I'm the one who was responsible for its implementation and answerable to the minister. I don't know to what extent I was able to assist you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A final question on this topic, although I shall return to it in another setting at the appropriate place in the chronology. But a final question, with a single word answer, if you can help us. Are you saying it was your idea alone to use this title and that you simply made it up; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer it in that way. Somewhere in the media I picked up this and I adopted it. Now, why the media presented it that way, I don't know, and I never thought about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is one supplementary question. We've heard a lot about the titles Mr. Kordic used, and you'll, I hope, take it from me that within the general time period that we're referring to, he's gone by the title of Vice-President of the Republic, and he's also gone by the title of Vice-President of Herceg-Bosna, and indeed vice-president of the party. Why didn't you use one of those three titles if you wanted to give him -- or if you wanted to give his signature particular authority? Perfectly available titles. Why not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: These events should be looked at in the light of how the media were presenting it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Your Honour, I'm going to go back to an earlier period and I'm going to take you through certain documents, I hope quite quickly. If you'll just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But before I do, there's one other thing I've got to say. Your job started when? In December of 1992, was it? I'll check.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: December of 1993, if you are referring to the position of the head of the Defence Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Who gave you or who appointed you to that job?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I was appointed by Dr. Jadranka Prlic, as the Prime Minister of the HVO government, the civilian HVO. He appointed me through a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Kordic one of those who was also instrumental in appointing you to your job?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know, and I cannot recall the exact procedure of nomination, how it went, because before my appointment I had been in Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 346, I think, please. Sorry, 345. I just want to see a few documents to have your comments on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that we have the picture, this is a document that is proposing appointments for the chiefs of the defence office, and the recommendation comes by Mr. Kordic, as Vice-President of HDZ BiH. And we can see that you've stamped and signed the document. What's his role in all that, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: That was the procedure which was in force at that time. Mr. Kordic just signed it, but without a stamp, because it was stamped by the municipal board of HDZ and by the municipal office in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But he signed this document, which is recommending, or proposing, the Chiefs of Staff of the defence office?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: That is just a proposal, and the head of the Defence Department could accept it or not. Any proposal of mine, also he had full right to accept or not accept. That was his right as the head of the Defence Department and later Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A similar document, Exhibit 346. I shan't produce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as far as timing is concerned, we'll adjourn at 5 past. We will return at 2.40. We cannot sit beyond 5 past 4:00, at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll be done within that period of time. As the Chamber will have foreseen, I've got a number of documents that this witness, whose name appears on many documents -- to put to him, but that's basically all I have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If, then, you could find a convenient moment about 5 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Your Honours, just give me a minute. 365, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that I shouldn't have troubled you with this document, but it's there before you. We'll deal with it shortly. This is a document of yours on the 16th of January of 1993. It certainly -- it reveals what sort of activities you were engaged in. This is a question of preparing lists of military conscripts who have left the municipality since 1992. And what we can see is that in January of 1993 -- I remember why I wanted to put it to you, or ask you to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Let me just look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were putting, or attempting to put, very considerable pressure on conscripts to return to the homeland and to defend the homeland, to register by the 22nd of February, warned through the media that they would be considered deserters if they failed to return and that they'd lose their properties. Do you remember sending this order?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that the document in front of me, the signature is mine, but the front is very poorly legible. I have to say that the -- in 1992 the war -- state of war was declared, and all military conscripts had to comply with the provisions of that state. So that was not pressure; that was part of my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who particularly gave you this instruction at the time? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I could only have received the instruction from the Defence Department --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because -- Blanked page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: -- and based on regulations which regulated this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because by the 16th of January, although there had been incidents, there was no, in any sense, full-scale battle with the Muslims by this stage, was there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: But we had areas which had been occupied by the BSA and the JNA in 1992. And in order to -- and the administration was established in January 1993, and we had to see what the situation was. We had to gain an insight and overview of what it was. About 50 per cent of the potential recruits had left. The crisis in the former Yugoslavia, the economic crisis, had started in the 1980s, so people were leaving the areas. And then the years of 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this: Was there, in fact, an expectation in the early or mid-part of January that you would be needing forces because you may be in conflict with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No. We did not have such estimates and we did not have such expectations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In January 1993 you were where? In Travnik or --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: As I mentioned, the office was in Vitez, from the time of the establishment, and I was involved in getting all the personnel. At first the administration consisted of myself and a seal which I kept in my pocket --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: So I really have no fill the positions in order to carry out the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question, perhaps, before the break, if that's convenient to the Court, is this: On the 20th of January things happened in neighbouring Busovaca, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was an aggression on Busovaca and Kiseljak. At that time, that weekend, I spent in Kresevo with my family, which I did on a regular basis. And then I was cut off there, and I believe that I was only able to get back to Vitez in March. And meanwhile I was able to carry out my duties in Kacuni and Bilalovac and later in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In January, on the 20th of January, attacks were made by the HVO on the Muslim interests in Busovaca, all as a result, it would appear, of an incident at a checkpoint in Kacuni. Do you accept that summary of events that I've just put to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No. Incidents were happening continuously throughout the area. We would have to go all the way back to 1992, because in 1992 we lost Ivica Stojak, our commander in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you accept the summary I've just put to you as for Busovaca on the 20th of January, 1993, please, Mr. Puljic? Do you accept that summary?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, I've drawn it --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't accept it as such because I don't know enough about the situation there. And to the extent that I know it, the events started much earlier. Incidents were going on throughout that period, and the specific event I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That might be a convenient moment. Mr. Puljic, would you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Defence team. Could you be back, please, at 2.40.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, I'm trying to get a full picture of matters that you can help us with. We've got some constraints on time so I'm going to deal with some documents very briefly. First of all, 551.1 and 551.2. As they're coming to you these are documents for the 18th of March of 1993. Do you accept that at that time, there were an increasing number of incidents involving criminal and destructive activity by individuals in HVO uniforms and that as a result of that, you reminded brigade commanders of their duty to deal with criminal behaviour by conscripts. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I have to see the document and comment only then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have a look at both the documents briefly, 551.1 sent at 8.00 in the morning to the defence offices of various municipalities, all right? Then if you'd like, I think just look at the heading of that or cast your eyes down it.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, but can you help me? What item did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The whole document. It's not very difficult. It's got a headline and it says, "Instructions on how to treat conscripts who act in a destructive and criminal matter." It says there is an increasing number of criminal behaviour and it then reminds people how to discipline such conscripts.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This document is an instruction to chiefs of offices saying that those members of the brigades who are demobilised for improper behaviour should be assigned to work; that is, that they should not be relieved of their duties in the war, but that they have to be separated because their conduct is dangerous, some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ...reports on what you were doing, you sent this half an hour later to Mr. Valenta and various other people. All right. Just look at that and then we can move on to the next document. Thank you, very much. The next document very briefly, 604.3 for the 5th of April. One of the things I'm going to be suggesting to you generally this afternoon, Mr. Puljic, is that there was, in reality, an almost independent part of Herceg-Bosna in your region. Its regional controller was Mr. Kordic, and that civilian and military matters were all integrated. I would be grateful if you'd have in mind that that is the suggestion, one of the suggestions I'm putting to you so that you can deal with it. This document is a 5th of April invitation, the Chamber won't remember, I shouldn't think, but -- I needn't trouble you with that. This document is an invitation by you to the chiefs of various municipal offices requiring their attendance at a 9th of April seminar and again, the topic of discussion included the establishment of defence offices but it also included organisation of the Central Bosnia zone armed forces. Now, doesn't this again reflect close integration of what you say is the civil side of the defence office and the armed forces themselves? Simple point and then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This document was not sent to different people, but to chiefs of municipal defence offices who were within the field of competence of the administration which I headed. The subject of the workshop was an order, if you remember, which I issued in March about the replenishment of units, mobilisation of men and replenishment of units. So I wanted them to report to me about what they had done regarding their regular duties which had to be complied with by that time. So this is -- this was it. How many men had been sent and mobilised on the basis of the -- pursuant to my previous instructions. I think that I issued those instructions sometime in mid-March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that document, again, is one we've seen before. It's the 8th of April. It's document 631. It's a big meeting that was held in Travnik on Maundy Thursday, the 8th of April, I think. The first page reveals with a steering committee of Kordic and others attended by, amongst other people, yourself, we can see you towards the top of the second page and there are only three quick points I want you to make about this meeting. First of all, do you remember the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I do remember the meeting because, among other things, it considered the political and security situation in Central Bosnia. That was the subject. It was a very broad meeting of political but also of the executive nature of the HVO. And I attended it in my capacity as the head of the administration at which we presented our ideas and our understanding of some of the topical problems at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The third page in the English version, in the Croatian version probably the third page as well under heading, "Excused Absence," it's just a tiny point but we can see, this connects to something we've heard Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. recently, it's actually on the second page in the Croatian version. It says that the representatives from Kiseljak and Kresevo were excused absence because of barricades set up by Muslims in Bilalovac and Kacuni. I remind the Judges that this is the 8th of April of 1993. If we go on to the next page -- well, first of all, do you remember that, the existence of barricades at Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I remember it very well, because after the conflict in January, that is, open aggression against Kiseljak and Busovaca, there was -- the communications were blocked and so that between Kiseljak and Busovaca, there was no -- I remember it very well because I simply couldn't get home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just since you've had the lunchtime to think about it, you can remember the open aggression, you say, against Busovaca and Kiseljak. Have you been able to recall, over the luncheon adjournment, the open aggression by the Croats against the Muslims in Busovaca or is that still lost to your memory?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This thing in Busovaca, well, you can see, you've just shown me the document showing that there were incidents, and we were taking certain actions in order to put an end to those incidents. It wasn't an open aggression. There was uncontrolled behaviour of some members of the HVO and throughout that process, not only this document specifically, but there were a number of measures that were taken and other brigades were taken -- taking certain disciplinary measures. But from what I learned that they were not bound to inform me. But since they were relieving some men of the duties in their brigades, then we were faced with the problem and so we issued the instructions in April that those men should be placed at the labour obligations, and weapons were taken away from them and so on and so forth. That is the weapons that belonged to the brigades. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The fourth page in the English, the third page in the Croatian, paragraph 5. You were at the meeting. It says this: That the meeting decided to give full support to Mr. Mate Boban for his superhuman efforts in resolving the historical destiny of the Croatian people. Was that destiny to live in an enlarged Croatian state, please? Is that what you understood by "the historical destiny of the Croatian people"?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No. The Bosnia-Herzegovinian crisis had been internationalised, and in 1992 talks had already begun about the solution to the Bosnia-Herzegovinian crisis. So I think this concerns -- this is about the support lent to Mr. Boban during the negotiations with the International Community, that is, the negotiations which comprised all three ethnic communities from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Passing over the next paragraph, I observe, just so the Chamber won't overlook it, that operation of HVO bodies includes a requirement for proportionally to include Muslims. But then we come to military organisation, and just note this, please, if you would. Under military organisation it says this: "Military authorities have to work as much as possible on strengthening the military organisation and full readiness for the defence of Croatian territory, and individuals must be appointed to key posts after consultation with the HDZ." Well, now, please help us, Mr. Puljic. You were a member of the HDZ, you were a member of the defence office, you knew about the army. It's right, isn't it, that the party, the civil side and the army, were all inextricably linked, as this little passage gives away.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: That is your opinion. My opinion is quite different. It is natural to seek the ablest personnel for different duties, regardless of whether one is talking about the military or the civilian part of life. One always looks for the best players.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: That is natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt you. The party, we know, established the community, the community established the HVO, all without a vote. You've now got the military part, as you would say, of the HVO. Why has the political party got to be consulted about military appointments if there isn't, in reality, a single body running things? Help me.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: The party did not appoint personnel at all, but it could be consulted about certain nominations. But it does not mean that these proposals -- that is, if party people proposed somebody, it was not who appointed them. The brigade commanders, the commander of the Operative Zone, did not have to go by the opinion of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, on page 7 of the English, and I think it will be the last page of the Croatian, which I'm going to summarise. There was a discussion at this meeting with representatives of Vares and Kakanj. And if we pick it up at the foot of the page in English and after the names listed, please, Mr. Puljic. "The views and the political opinion of Boban were conveyed, and the representatives of Vares and Kakanj gave their full support and thanks to President Boban and the delegation for their attempts to restore the two municipalities to the borders of the Croatian province." What's meant by "Croatian province," please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: The negotiations -- I think this is Vance-Owen Plan negotiations -- when the municipalities Vares and Kakanj found themselves outside the municipalities with a Croat majority. They were here in a minority. But those negotiations had not come to an end. Because as far as I can remember, the Croat side did sign these papers, but they had not come to an end. And this is how one should interpret this, as an attempt at a further effort. What if the plan does not go through? Because in the past we had a number of negotiations and plans which we accepted, but they never went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could you give me the exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. 631 for this exhibit. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the reference to the military organisation, which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It comes on page 4 and it's at the foot of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the registrar please come and have a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As we part from this document, which we can see on the last page is signed by Mr. Kordic as Colonel Kordic, and on this occasion as vice-president of the party, can you help at all with why he's signing himself as Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. On the last page you'll see that Mr. Kordic has signed "Pukovnik," Colonel. Can you help? Maybe you can't. Why is he signing as Colonel, especially when he's just there for the party? Do you see what I mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Sir, since tripartite talks were organised in Sarajevo under the umbrella of UNPROFOR, I believe it was all organised and run by General Morillon, and those talks were taking place at the airport in Sarajevo. In the beginning Mr. Kordic did not attend at those negotiations, but then he was given a role and participated in those negotiations. And I believe this was just a nominal function, because he was never in the command of any unit nor in the chain of command, so that this was merely a title, simply because of the problems with communications in late 1992 and early 1993. Because of the aggravated security situation, officers of the Main Staff could not attend these talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You seem to have been at pains to make out that he genuinely was a politician and had no desire really to be in any way military. Even assuming that what you say by way of the purpose for the title is correct, which I don't accept, the limited purpose of the title, why on earth should he be using it now? Those meetings were all over, the Sarajevo meetings. Why stick with the title "Colonel" unless this was a way of reflecting his real power in the region? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I do not think that the purpose of this signature -- that could not be the purpose of the signature, because Mr. Kordic could not order anything to be executed at that time. He had no authority regarding the command of the armed forces. I do not know why this is indicated in this paper, because I did not take part in wording this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'd accept, I suppose, would you, that it must be a different thing for somebody to sign himself as a colonel over a political job title; it's a different thing, isn't it, for that than, for example, signing himself a colonel in respect of the Operative Zone for Central Bosnia. You'd say there was a difference, would you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: From what I know about the armed forces, if somebody was a commander at a certain level, then it would mean that his order was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't got time to explore that anymore. The next document, 653.3, please, 14th of April. Here you are. Civil only side of the defence office. The document dated the 14th of April, signed by you, and stamped. And it goes to the chief of Vitez, Skopljak. "Following a tour of inspection of the Vitez Brigade, we were warned that the brigade has not been brought up to strength. Since all the deadlines for completion of the task contained in an order have expired, we're advising you to complete the task by the 22nd of April." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Is that really a civil instruction? It looks a bit military, it may be thought.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This absolutely is a civilian instruction, and it was defined when this task was to be completed. But after the tour of inspection in the Vitez Brigade, conducted by the operations on command, we intervened and we said that the task should be done as first set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We come to the incidents at Ahmici. Do you know anything about those?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: What I can say about it is that I was not directly informed about the events in Ahmici. I think that I was only informed about it two days after it happened. And I gave certain tasks to the defence office, that is, for the clearing of terrain to do the proper burials. I didn't realise what the proportions of these things were, and it was not within the scope of my job anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I dare say, but when did you discover what happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I did not discover. I received information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you receive information?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I was advised. Through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here you are, head of the defence office, with all the little defence offices -- not little -- all the other defence offices subordinate to you, close to Kordic and everybody else, and are you really telling us that you never found out directly anything about what happened at Ahmici, a hundred people killed and all that sort of thing? You never found out?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I talk about the first information I received. That was from the media. And the responsibility of the defence office, that was within the front. We were not competent for the troops. They were under no obligation to report to us, those who were in that zone of responsibility where that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to pass from this but I will just give you one chance. Some people will think it was the topic of interest at some stage and that people would want to ask. Did you ever ask to find out what happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Of course as a human being and as a person with some responsibility, I was interested, and after I received the first information -- but I never received any official reports. I tried to get information at the Operative Zone and the civilian protection when it was able to enter the area. That is the defence office because do not forget, there was fighting going on in that area for two or three days so they couldn't get in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help us and the Chamber and the Judges and so on. Can you help us please with who did the massacre? Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I cannot because I don't know -- even to date, I don't know and I never had access to the official information who -- which units were there. I never had the duty and the obligation to know which units were responsible for which zone of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Fine, if that's your answer, next question. Can we look at, please, Exhibit 2812A. This is for the 17th of April, you see this is just after Ahmici and it's a document that comes to you from Gavro Maric. And it's on the ELMO. We can see a little bit about it. It's for your attention and it says this, "We sent a report yesterday," so that would have been the 16th, "in which we informed you of two soldiers from Vitez killed in the conflict with Muslim forces. Last night, 16 April at 8.30 in the evening another was brought in, here are the names." There are three names. There is obviously something wrong with the years of birth, because even if the two at 1970 could possibly be accurate as they could be in 1993, the one in 1997 is plainly mistyped. So -- or something wrong about that but never mind. Then it goes on to say, since the Busovaca municipality --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: It is possible. I think that just one figure was added. It is possible that it was 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. "Since the Busovaca municipality has no conditions for preserving bodies of the deceased for longer periods, we ask you to inform the command and organs of the Vitez municipality since we weren't able to get in touch." Now, two or three things. First, what this document is revealing is that soldiers from Vitez had been found in some way dead or taken dead to Busovaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: It probably is correct because the person probably would not have reported the deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second thing is: We see that there is no complaint, there is no outrage in this report about how these men died, just simply records that we died in a conflict with the Muslim forces. Do you now recall, since there was apparently a discussion the night before, do you recall where these men died, please? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know, nor can I glean from the report at what part of the front they were killed. All I could do was ask the chief of defence office to see what he could do, and he said he would deal with it the next day and I presume that he dealt with it on the basis of this document, but I do not remember the specific situation. At that time, there was a lot of those killed. Civilians were getting killed and the situation was chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My position is this on the 16th of April, the HVO mounted an attack, and in the course of that, some of its soldiers got killed and the tone of in document fits with that, you see?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know where these soldiers were killed, at what front line. That's number one, I don't know. And second, we were attacked and I don't know whether they were killed at Ahmici or some other part of the front, I don't know, because the front around Vitez was about 70 kilometres long. But I cannot see from this report, and it wasn't my duty to know what part of the front line someone was killed at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document I want you to reconsider very briefly is 696. This is the document where you -- I will just remind the Chamber of it, this is where you used Mr. Kordic's name, Mr. Kostroman's name without their consent. They had no part in this document at all; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That is what I stated previously. But we can agree about this document. If -- especially if you considered their attitudes, their humanism and their human qualities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course I understand. And you are writing here to Colonel Stewart who is a stranger to your -- the intricacies of your organisation; would that be correct? He wouldn't know one way or another whether it would be likely for Mr. Kordic or Mr. Kostroman to sign this document so he would be happy to see your names there; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I never had an opportunity to meet Mr. Stewart, and I didn't have contacts with the international organisations and their representatives, but we were -- in the situation where there were combat operations going on, and I just try to protect the civilians. That is the import and that is the -- that was the aim of this document. I never had an opportunity to talk with Colonel Stewart personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is part of what you were doing at the time on orders and on behalf of others? Was part of what you were doing exaggerating the Croat suffering because it was already known that there had been unacceptable behaviour at Ahmici? Is that part of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Let me see the date here, 17 April. I had information, reports that large numbers of civilians from Zenica was on the move. Also we had a lot of people on the move in the municipality of Vitez so it was a general confusion. I did not have information on Ahmici. Had I had, I would have undertaken certain steps --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: -- within my -- the scope of my job, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, would you accept that it would be one thing to use Mr. Kordic's name when you are writing to a British battalion officer without Kordic's consent. It would, of course, be an entirely different thing to use Kordic's name or Kostroman's when writing to some senior Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. member of the HVO or the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you didn't understand I'll repeat it again. You couldn't possibly justify using Mr. Kordic's name without his consent if you were going to write to Mr. Boban, for example, you couldn't possibly justify doing that, could you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I did not need to send such letters. If the situation dictated that, I would have written a similar letter to Mr. Boban if the situation was such that the protection was needed for the population regardless of their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There would be no way of -- you couldn't justify borrowing Kordic's name when writing to Kordic's immediate superior, could you, without Kordic's consent. It would be terribly embarrassing because Boban would say to him, "I've just got your letter," and he'd say, "What letter?" You couldn't possibly justify that, could you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Again, let me repeat, I would have written such letter to Mr. Boban, and I believe that one such letter was sent by me to Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You understand the point that's coming. Exhibit 697, please. Indeed you did, on the same day, write to -- in fact, Mr. Petkovic, Boban, Stojic and others in similar terms and you signed for Kordic and for Kostroman. There's the letter. The translation can go on the ELMO. Similar terms following the massacre, organised evacuation, circular defence. You signed the letter, again, for all three. You did it with their consent as you well know.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No. I did not ask their consent for this letter either. The communications were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were they, Mr. Kordic and Mr. Kostroman on the day after Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I know that they were not in Vitez, and I know that they were headquartered in Busovaca so I assume that they were there. I know that they couldn't have come to Vitez because of the fighting that was going on in the area and the communications were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they communicate with you and tell you to send this letter, in particular, Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see I'm going to suggest that this was part of planned defence by the HVO to what it knew was coming by way of adverse comments, understating it, adverse views once Ahmici was discovered. Do you accept that? This was all part of defensive reaction by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say -- it's not a document of yours, I'll just identify for it for its number, 701.1. Did you know, at the time on the 17th of April, somebody named Tomic? Did you know somebody called Tomic was asserting that UNPROFOR was siding with Muslim forces and opening fire on Croatian houses? Did you know that sort of disinformation was being circulated?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I hear that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: You said that there was a document, can I see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly you can see it but it's not yours. It's 701.1.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: If it's not my document then perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'll see --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This is from the Operative Zone command. I had nothing to do with them. That was part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Incidentally, were you aware, and this is another document that you can look at if you'd like, it comes from Blaskic but it's not yours. The document is 702. Were you aware that at the same day, the 17th of April, although Blaskic was complaining of Croats in Zenica suffering at Muslim hands, he was also saying that all of today's attacks had been repelled and the enemy had been crushed. Were you aware of that and was it true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know because I did -- I was not in the possession of information regarding the situation of our forces on the front line. During this confusion, Mr. Blaskic was at his command post, and I didn't ask any information from him and he was not under any obligation to send any to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we'll come now, please, to the 2nd of June, Exhibit 1009. This is a document addressed to you. It comes from Colonel Kordic, vice-president of the community dated the 2nd of June, and it's a decision. What it says is this: "In compliance with a verbal agreement in Novi Travnik, the defence office will allocate these are forcibly taken vehicles as follows and one to Stjepan Tomasevic, one to the Novi Travnik HVO, and the third to the 4th Military Police Battalion." That shows, as clear as can be, that Kordic had authority with all branches of the military, doesn't it? He could allocate, seize resources between competing claimants.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What else does it show?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I can only understand this decision as information, and I think that these allocations were already -- had already been carried out and this is just as a follow-up, this information. To me, I perceive this more as information not as an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who else made the decision as it is headed if it wasn't Mr. Kordic, please, in respect of, I remind you, Stjepan Tomasevic, Novi Travnik and the 4th Military Police Battalion. Who else was it? Who else had authority over all three?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I explained the process of mobilisation. In their -- the brigades went to those who were in -- competent for their zone of responsibility so that in Novi Travnik, they went to the Novi Travnik defence office. In Vitez, the Vitez defence office and so on, and they would be then given whatever was available to that office at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a simple question and then I'm going to move on: Who, as a single person, who had authority over those three groups if not Mr. Kordic? Can you name anyone else; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: In mobilisation, there wasn't a single person. I was responsible for the mobilisation not only those three municipalities, but including those three municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Exhibit 1135, example of Kordic's control over you. This is the 2nd of July, and in his office of vice -- in his office as -- he signs "Vice-President of the Office of the President of HR HB." Note that, please. A different title: Vice-President of the Office of the President of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Now, the president of Herceg-Bosna had military authority, and he's now signing as vice-president. And the order is about conscripts and new recruits and training courses. That's not a civilian order; that's a military order, isn't it? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This is a civilian order. This concerns the enrollment of people in military registers, their recruitment, and their dispatch for military training. Because this is the young generation, and in times of crisis we could also engage people of that age group. If you look at the decree, then you will understand why this is so. This is not a military order; this is a civilian order, because it is addressed to the Defence Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then I'm going to suggest that actually what you're talking is frankly nonsense. But perhaps you'll help us with this and answer that suggestion of mine as well. Why is he now signing as Vice-President of the Office of the President?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Well, listen, that is something that I don't know. It skipped -- I received this letter from them. I cannot explain that. But under the decree of the armed forces, this is the president. So perhaps because the communications with Mr. Boban were cut off and the decision had to be taken, because we were faced with a shortage of men in the units and we had to carry out additional mobilisation. [Indiscernible] -- that document on the basis of which we could do it, so regular sending of recruits for training, that is normally done under peacetime conditions, and not to mention the situation in which we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can see the time, so I'm pruning a number of documents. I may come back to them, but probably not. If you'll just give me a minute, I'll be able to sort my thinking out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1198.3, the 9th of September. This is a document coming to you from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document is dated the 9th of September, Blaskic to you, informing you that the following members of the Vitezovi Special Purpose Unit are to be put at the disposal of the Travnik Defence Administration in the Vitez forward command post, and the men are all listed. That means, doesn't it, that they're to be put at the disposal of the Vitez Brigade, is that right, or have I got it wrong?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No. This came from the Operational Zone Central Bosnia, that is, Colonel Blaskic, and he informs me which military conscripts had been relieved of duty in Vitezovi and tells us what municipalities they come from so that I could make a list and give it to the heads of defence offices in Travnik, Vitez --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These soldiers would then have been working --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: -- and also those who were from Zenica, because they were under the defence office in Vitez; that is, because they were now available, that they should be sent to brigades which were short of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: For instance, in Travnik, there were two brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Regular interchange of troops --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Regular interchange of troops between special patrol units -- special units and other units; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No. These are military conscripts. They were relieved, had no duties in their units. So they are placed at the disposal of the defence office, and the defence office decide where it will assign them to. I cannot see from this whether they were under disciplinary proceedings or something. This could be labour obligation for these men. But since they all seem to be of young age, possibly they were to be sent to some other units. So this was sending men from units to civilians. And may I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I want. Thank you very much. Z1253. We've already looked at documents in September, where Kordic was given the title of head of the forward command post of the president. This is another document. This time it goes from you to the defence minister himself, your supreme boss. It encloses some orders and it just simply says this: "The above orders were issued by the head of the Travnik Defence Administration, Mr. Anto Puljic, with the approval of the following ..." Starting in reverse order, Valenta. He's there as his HVO position; Kostroman, his position of Secretary-General of the Republic, as it was called; and then Colonel Dario Kordic, head of the forward command post of the office of the HR HB president. You typed it, or you had it typed, and you signed it. What did you mean by it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: In my explanation to your earlier question, I told you about this order. This was the information that I was sending to Mr. Bruno Stojic, defence minister of HR HB, about the defence office in Vitez. And I also pointed out here that, as it was shown in the media, I put the title next to Mr. Kordic's name. I do not know if he ever used it when he corresponded with me in official correspondence. I simply used what was being used in the media at the time, because -- at press conferences and so on and so forth. So this wasn't formal. And this document was written by me, or rather I signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please explain what is the IZM forward command post of which Colonel Kordic was the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you answer the Judge's question, please. What was the IZM, please? I think it actually is forward command post. I think its expansion is forward command post.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This acronym, it was used mostly in the units of the Croat Defence Council, Main Staff, commander of the Operational Zone, brigade commander, and that is commander in a certain area of responsibility. And I think in this communication, as it was always in the media, then somebody used the IZM. And I told about that to Mr. Kordic, but I do not think he discharged that duty, because he did not have that command authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: An order could be issued only by the commander within the armed forces, or rather our Main Staff. And everybody has common knowledge who he received the orders from, that is, the chief of the Main Staff. I hope, Your Honour, that you are satisfied with this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wanted to know if the command post, is that the military command, military command post?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No, no. No, no, no. By no means. By no means. Not in this case. I really wouldn't know either. Let me tell you, it was in the media all the time: forward command post, certain commanders of military units, and then somebody used simply in the media "forward command post" for Mr. Kordic. But Mr. Kordic couldn't have it, because all the institutions worked in accordance with the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Puljic, but it is you who signed this document. This is not something that was done in the media. So you approved that title, forward command post. You signed this document. How could it be, then? How could you use it in the document? I'm asking you, Mr. Puljic.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I've just -- I'm saying I simply used it because it was in the media already, because I never received it in any official document from Mr. Kordic that he discharged that duty. But I'm saying as it was always in the media and then I wrote the order and the previous document, the document which preceded this one, and because of which I was sending the report to the minister, then I simply put it because of what the media said, as media put it. But that was not his official office, because I did not receive any official document, so I cannot say. If somebody made Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. an omission, then the omission was mine, not Mr. Kordic's. And this document was written and I approved it and it was signed by my deputy. But I stand by this document. I am the person responsible for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me be blunt. The account you're giving is untrue, and you're giving it in order to try and protect Kordic, as is revealed by the fact, if you like, that this document itself is headed "military secret". These are military matters, and you know it perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the defence department, we had not only rules on job distribution, but also we had some rules on the protection of the confidentiality of documents. And we behaved accordingly. That was how we recorded the documents in the books and also ex officio we had to put defence up there in order to protect the confidentiality of these documents. Because after all, there was war and war activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look briefly at 1290 which is dated the 9th of November. A small point. It's headed, "Military Secret" dated the 9th of November, about evacuation of inhabitants and it's signed by you. It deals with Kiseljak. You sent it, quite specifically, to the office of the vice-president of the Republic, Mr. Dario Kordic, personally. He was the vice-president and he was, for practical purposes, in your region, the authority; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This document was the result of the difficult situation and developments in Vares, because a huge number of refugees had arrived in Kiseljak and some were still on their way there from Vares through Ilijas to Kiseljak. And in this letter I am asking to provide accommodation for people who were on the run, to ensure their safest possible evacuation. Because in the dramatic situation the head of the office --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so pressed for time, I'm going to have to cut you short, because I've only got another ten minutes and I've got some important documents to put to you that you must deal with. I want to know simply an answer to this question. You sent it to Mr. Kordic as vice-president of the Republic because that's what he was. And I'd like you, while you're thinking about this question, to look at 1316. It will save some time. This is an assignment proposal of a military nature, somebody who was a corporal being proposed for another job, and it comes from three people, one of whom is Mr. Kordic, again signing as vice-president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic, it says here, but I'm not really sure if at that time he was -- he held the office of the vice-president. But I put his name in this document and I wrote this document and explained why. But he didn't have it. I repeat: He had the political role, but none in the executive power nor civilian nor the military one. And the document that you show to me is my proposal for the assignment of my deputy, Ljubomir Jurcic, to -- and his assignment to a job in the Ministry of Defence. And I'm asking Mr. Dario Kordic and Mr. Kostroman to give their opinion of him, and they signed it. This is a proposal to the defence minister --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: -- for a job in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you can't explain why he signed as vice-president of the republic, can you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Not at this moment, because it was in the media always and I'm not sure that he was the vice-president of the republic. I know that he was the vice-president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna but not of the Croat republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1317.1, this is a very short document. It doesn't relate to Mr. Kordic. It's a document signed by you on the 27th of November. I just want to know, please, whether this was standard behaviour and performance. You requested 300 tonnes of coal under the guise of humanitarian assistance to organise the production of gun powder and rocket fuel. Which humanitarian group did you persuade to provide you with this coal; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I was not trying to talk anyone into anything. I sent this document saying that we needed this coal, not only as industrial fuel but in Vitez, there was a factory and the boiler room was also used to heat the town because this is winter and we needed heating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It says, "under the guise of humanitarian assistance." Which humanitarian organisation did you attempt to persuade to provide you with this coal, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Me? None.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: But I wasn't trying to persuade them about it because that was not my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One thing we know, because you've confirmed it this morning, is that the main staff is a military organisation. So I'd like you to look at some documents, and because we are so pressed for time I may have to ask you to look at them very quickly. 1357.2, please first. Once the documents are in, their content can be the subject of argument at later stages in the trial. 14th of January 1994, you sign and send a letter to, amongst others, Mr. Kordic in his capacity as assistant chief of the main staff. Do you see that document?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I do have the document. We organised a system of communications. Let me just explain. Until that time, we were using the communications system of the Operative Zone Central Bosnia to send our documents. Meanwhile, we managed to obtain the equipment and established our system of communications, and here I inform that the civilian segment and that was the custom and the practice to send government documents to be sent through this particular system.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: That was the practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You answered me this morning, maybe when you didn't know what I was going to be asking you later, but you made it quite plain that the main staff was an exclusively military body. No ifs and buts, Mr. Puljic, that's what you told me. Now, let's look at another document, and this one is 1363. Can we have that? You can have them all, as far as I'm concerned. 25th of January, 1994. This is to do with gun powder production and it goes to Sliskovic and it goes to the assistant chief to the main staff of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Dario Kordic. Would you like to look next, please, at 1363.1? There's a shortage of time. This is dated the 26th of January, 1994. It's a document signed by you to be delivered to the assistant chief of the main staff, Colonel Dario Kordic. And indeed, it says that, "Based on an oral request from Colonel Dario Kordic," you've appointed a working group. Keeping those documents before you, we'll go to 1365.2, please. Dated the 2nd of February of 1994. It goes to the chief of the political administration of defence, Kostroman, and to the assistant chief of the main staff of the armed forces, Dario Kordic. And it's to do with the opinion on the creation of the Zenica defence office. 1369, please. The 9th of February, 1994. The content I'm not particularly concerned with. It comes from you, and it says at the top, hand over to the assistant chief of the general staff, the main staff of the armed forces, Colonel Dario Kordic personally in Busovaca. Z1371, please. This time, it's a document coming from Blaskic so it's not just by you, it's signed by him. And it's dated the 11th of February, but we see in the order on the first page in the English, and we can see the same thing in the first page towards the top in the Croatian this: "On the 9th of February at 1500 hours, a meeting was held in the military district command with the following participants: Colonel Dario Kordic, assistant chief of the HVO main staff," and others. And then finally on this topic, 1388.1, and after this, I only have two documents to do, and I think I've got -- well, the Court has only until ten past four. This is the 1st of March of 1994 and it goes from you. It's to do with helicopter access. "Attention the assistant chief of the general staff HR HB, the main staff of the armed forces, Colonel Dario Kordic in Busovaca." Right. Those are your documents save for the one from Blaskic which simply fits with yours. Can you tell me please, why he's addressed in an absolutely clear military capacity?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I was writing to Mr. Kordic because, as a politician, he wanted to receive the information about everything that happened. But all those extraordinary situations that I thought he should be informed, I simply sent him those letters to inform him. And on the other hand, I just say, as for the title, I used what is in the media. I do not know that he was not -- I do not know that he ever issued any order as the assistant chief of the main staff. So that I do not know that -- I do not know that he could issue orders to any unit, nor would it ever be carried out. And after all, Mr. Kordic -- Mr. Kordic became the president of the HDZ and otherwise, he would have been continued normally as Blaskic in the main -- through the main staff had he been a soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, you were an official of this organisation in charge of the defence administration department. You were writing to your superiors or, indeed, to Mr. Kordic himself. And do you really say that you were using a title which you had seen in the media? Why would you do such a thing?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is what I'm saying. I mean in the office which I held I was never notified officially that Mr. Kordic had been appointed, nor was I told about appointments in the main staff or the defence ministry except insofar as the service for which I was responsible was concerned. Besides, the communications were cut off, and the first time I could talk -- seven, no ten months after I was appointed, I met my minister for defence because of the communications problem, I simply couldn't meet anyone. So I'm talking about the communication problems we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you used the title which you had seen in the media; is that what we are to believe?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I came here to tell the truth and this is what I did, how I lived, and what I lived through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We haven't had those exhibits unless they are previously exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I think they have mostly been previously exhibited, and I have been distributing the new ones as they've come along.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You do realise, Mr. Puljic, that this is the second title you've picked up from the press, you're saying, not just one, two titles that you are simply borrowing from the media; is that really your account?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I've just said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which media?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Media which were accessible to us at the time; local television, local press.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So may we take it then that the local press, on your account, was describing him as the deputy president or was describing him as the deputy head of the main staff and they were never corrected and they just carried on using these incorrect terms. Is that really your position?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't really keep up with the media because of my daily obligations, but what I could see on those occasion when I had opportunity to follow the media, that was what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the most three, probably only two other documents. The first one, 327.1, we go back in time. The reality, Mr. Puljic, is that you owe a lot to Mr. Kordic because, indeed, he got you your job. It's on the 18th of December 1992, which is incorrect, it should be the 28th. It's been translated at speed and in error. The recommendation that Anto Puljic should take his job as the chief of the office of defence having taken active part in the work of the HVO for the first days of the war, having been a founding member of the HDZ, and having held the office as president in Kresevo, should have this job. And there you were, you were put up for it by vice-president of the HZ HB and the HVO, Colonel Dario Kordic, along with Blaskic and Kostroman. Do you remember that now?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This morning I said that I was not familiar with the procedure of my appointment, rather how I was suggested or nominated. And I'm happy to see this document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware that in -- on the 7th of October of 1993 when you were away from the area, there was a meeting where efforts were made to unseat you, to remove you from your position? Mr. Vidak, in particular, was concerned to get you out of your post; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I do remember, yes. I was informed about it, and I did see the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it Kordic who kept you your job on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I think it was kept for me by the defence minister because if he thought that I should have been removed, then he would have removed me regardless of what Mr. Kordic's opinion might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The very last document out of order. I just want your comment on 1189.1. It's a document of yours. It's out of sequence. 1st of September 1993. I just want your comment on this. It fits with an earlier question I asked you. It says this, "The Croatian people in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are waging a defence war that has been imposed on them by the enemy. The enemy of the Croatian people is anybody who threatens their existence and the territorial integrity of their state." Which state?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or was it the smaller state or was it the state of Croatia itself of which you were primarily concerned?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No. We were primarily concerned about Bosnia-Herzegovina because you may have noticed that all the documents that I wrote had above the letterhead Bosnia-Herzegovina and all the seals that they used, and these documents also bore Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, and I apologise for the briskness of the pace I've had to move at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have even less time at my disposal, but I will really try to -- not to go beyond a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, there was mention about the titles that you used when you -- which titles you added to the name of Mr. Kordic. The Prosecutor says two, and it seems to me that there were three titles in these documents that we were showing you. Their Honours also asked you what does "IZM" mean and you gave us your view. However, the second word which is next to it is not said and it says IZM office or chancellery and "kancelarija" or "chancellery," it means office, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Was the word "chancellery" used to describe the military command or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So when we say "chancellery," it means office?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Which part of the government is called chancellery?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Well, it can be minister's office or prime minister and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Or to put it this way, the word "chancellery" or "office," do they exist in military or civilian branches of power?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Only in civilian branches of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You spoke about a forward command post, your office was also relocated, that is, it was not a command post. It was simply a forward post; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said this morning in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So it was relocated because you did not work in Travnik. You worked from another town, from Vitez, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So when one says "relocated", it does not mean command.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: That is what I am trying to explain to Their Honours. Yes, relocated, that is what it means. But this "IZM", I don't know about the terminology but the word that has been used was relocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell the Court, where was Mr. Kordic's, that is Mr. Kostroman's office? Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: They were located in Busovaca on the premises of Ivancica, a lodge in Tisovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And was there a military command there or an office or a chancellery as we have just said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to make sure I understand the point you are making about the reference to "kancelarija". I have here Z1253 and I can see in the Croatian the reference to kancelarija after IZM. Is this your case that what is referred to here is a civilian office and not a military office?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, you are absolutely right, Your Honour, because this "IZM" means "relocated post". It does not mean a "relocated command post". As Mr. Puljic just said, he was head of the defence administration in Travnik, but he did not work in the town of Travnik but in a relocated place in Vitez. I believe he told us so this morning. And he was not with the military command, he was in the civilian wing of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And just one thing. I believe there was a certain misunderstanding here, and I will explain where it was. Tell us, please: When were you appointed head of the Travnik Defence Administration?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: In early January 1993, and I was relieved of that office in June, at my request, in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And for the record, I'm saying because on page 46, line 16, it says that you were there from November 1993, when asked by the Prosecutor, but I think that was an error.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: No. It could have been a proposal for my -- it could have been a proposal for my appointment, could have been -- could have happened in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Z1090. It here says, and perhaps -- this is perhaps not quite precise: Mr. Puljic said the office of the deputy president relocated, and you say Mr. Dario Kordic [as interpreted]. So you're writing to him as a political figure. And then in the text you say -- you speak about refugees from Vares, in the last paragraph: "Will you please take political and all other measures to resolve the status of refugees." Is that what you wanted to explain the honour [as interpreted], why you were sending it to those persons?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And I have to be very quick. Z345. This document you are proposing to your superior to appoint a certain person to the office of the head of the defence office in Travnik. And here some men are listed, and consent given by, and you list certain names, and Mr. Kordic included.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: This was a practice we followed when proposing, when nominating individual people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So the question is: Mr. Ivica Markovic, was he being proposed for a civilian or for a military post?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Civilian, because the head of the civilian administration is a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. And I suppose the same applies to Z1209, where they agree to your text regarding two developments in Vitez, both Ignac Kostroman and Valenta, and Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: May I just see the document?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: But I suppose that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What are these offices, civilian or military? The defence offices, what are they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Civilian. Civilian, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This is the document Z1208. If you don't have it, don't look for it, because I think we've -- you've told us a great deal about this already, so there is no need to go into it. But this is only a consent. 1208. And it again means consent [as interpreted]. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: I emphasise that this order to -- if I had a lesser political climate -- and the Prosecutor has just shown records -- in assessing the situation and the reaction that this order might provoke. Because in view of the general developments, and that is why I sought this consent. I am responsible, and I was the person who could put it through. But that was the only reason why I sought it. But when I seek support -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Who are the officials that you seek support from?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: From amongst those who are in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: That is, do you seek the support the civilians or the military?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Civilians, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Many documents were shown, various letters that you write to Mr. Kordic. Some pertain to technical documentation, some concern the establishment of the defence office in Zenica, and so on and so forth. Now, the question is: In your view, are these military matters, in the strict sense of the word, or is this a different kind of content in these documents?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Since Mr. Kordic was a man of politics, I asked for his opinion, his view, because meaning whether the political moment is opportune, is convenient, to go into certain activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My last question to you, Mr. Puljic. There was talk about different titles that you used when writing to Mr. Kordic. Did you ever hear that by the end of the war, that is, spring of 1994, did Mr. Kordic discharge any duty in the Main Staff of the HVO in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic never discharged any duty in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Puljic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. We'll adjourn now until --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two housekeeping matters, as they're described. First -- I'll just wait for the witness to withdraw. I know the Chamber is pressed for time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shan't be here on Monday and Tuesday, but I've made arrangements, both with those who will be conducting the case for the Prosecution and with the Defence, that if the witness Petkovic comes, he won't be called till Wednesday, although we'd be grateful for his summary, which must have been prepared, because he was going to be the first witness, I think, originally, as the Chamber will recall. We'd be grateful for his summary, draft or otherwise, immediately. The second point is that there's affidavits outstanding. Now, we've prepared our usual document. There were four affidavits we objected to. We don't make any particular points in relation to two. But if they can be put off generally till next Wednesday. Of course, if other witnesses have to be called, they'll have to be deposed in the Cerkez case, but that would probably have had to happen in any event. So if you're content for the matter to be put off until my return next Wednesday, I'd be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do that. Let us have, please, the document, then, so we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The grounds for objection for the first two haven't been articulated particularly, but the matters that are covered have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Sayers, if you could send your usual batting order to us, we'd be grateful. We have not dealt with the affidavits, but we will next Wednesday, or whenever is convenient after that. We have to deal with the transcripts. We also have to deal with your outstanding exhibits next week. Are you in a position to tell us how many witnesses you're going to call or is that still a matter which is in doubt?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We're confident that Witness DK can be completed on Monday morning. We're relatively confident that the second witness will be, (redacted). We're less confident that -- our third witness will be Colonel Marinko Palavra. I'm afraid we're even less confident of that, that our last witness will indeed testify live as opposed to by transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll certainly have work for Monday and probably Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wednesday we can either have a witness or we'll go into the legal argument. It might be helpful if you would prepare something, even if it's oral, but a paper, as to exactly what's in your exhibits. I mean, I don't want a detailed breakdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. What we propose to do is this, in a nutshell, Mr. President. We're going to file a document which lists all of the exhibits that we've introduced so far. Then we'll file a summary of each of the individual binders that we've submitted to Trial Chambers, which lets you know what's in there. There are going to be two more volumes which will be submitted. I regret to say that we came across about a roomful of UNPROFOR documents which we had to go through over the course of the last week, and we've culled about I think two binders full of UNPROFOR documents. But I can't imagine that there's going to be any objection to those. And those will be filed, as I said, Thursday or Friday. But you should have an index of all of the binders and that should make it fairly easy to analyse their contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good. We'll sit again on Monday, half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: reconvened on Monday the 17th day of July, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
